newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Unrest, looting spread to Albania's north.
newsitem.headline: Unrest, looting spread to Albania's north.

text.p: Albania's chaotic armed insurgency spread through the north of the country on Thursday as looters raided military bases for weapons and forced police to release prisoners from the cells.
Repeated bursts of gunfire, as looters loosed off their rifles into the air, could be heard all along the road north from Tirana, itself the scene of looting and shooting in the last 24 hours.

Unlike rebels in the south who have taken over towns to demand the resignation of President Salih Berisha after they lost their savings in collapsed pyramid investment shemes, the northerners seemed just to want guns for self-protection.
Northerners had seen their southern cousins seizing arms in a climate of growing lawlessnes and now wanted to do the same as the state's power to protect them melted away, local people said.

In the town of Lezhe, a ruling Democratic Parrty stronghold 70 km (45 miles) north of Tirana, armed youths on motorcyles and in cars patrolled the streets repeatedly firing their looted Kalashnikov assult rifles into the air.
In nearby Lac, a crowd of several hundred people, many armed, gathered outside the police station where relatives were demanding the release of about 40 prisoners held there.
Eventually the police decided it would be safer for them to release the prisoners rather than risk a confrontation.

Previously untouched by the revolt sweeping the south, much of Albania along the main highway leading north has now turned into an area where the cvilians are rapidly becoming better armed than the soldiers.

A constant stream of men, women and boys passed along the road leading from the town's military base, bearing away guns, ammunition, medical supplies, clothing and anything else they could find. Cars, bicycles, donkeys and tractors were pressed into service to carry away the spoils.
Nikoll, an unemployed man with a Kalashnikov slung across his back and engaged in rolling away a stolen truck wheel, said he had no more food and no more money.
"Unfortunately we Albanians have failed to be international champions in basketball and football," he said. "But we can at least be champions at looting."
He added: "We are the new Chechens now."
Along the road, petrol station owners posted armed guards to deter looters as young boys drove donkeys loaded with boxes of stolen ammunition away from raided barracks.
Police looked on without taking action and the few soldiers in evidence either did nothing or asked for money to pay their busfare back to Tirana.

George Makaj, who had returned to Albania "for a rest" last year after working for nearly 10 years in the United States, latterly in a 7-11 convenience store in San Diego, California, felt matters could only get worse.
"I do believe we are on the brink of a civil war," he said.
In Lezhe, people hurriedly bought large sacks of flour and a local merchant said he had sold seven tonnes already on Thursday.

But in Tirana, people took more direct action to safeguard their food supplies. Hundreds of residents of the capital, many of them armed, looted a Swiss-owned warehouse, using bicycles, wheelbarrows and donkeys, as well as their own backs, to carry away sacks of flour.
